title: 私の店にします  (Buying the Bookstore)

segments.t: Next, Muranishi walks into a quiet Sapporo bookstore run by Kitamori and tries to place his magazines on the shelves. When Kitamori refuses, Muranishi unzipping his leather bag turns a rejected pitch into an unexpected job offer. Listen to their exchange in Japanese first without worrying about every detail.
どうぞ。
こちらのお店には置いてありませんね。
いや、別に興味はありません。
隠さなくて結構ですよ。
ちょっと待ってください！
うちではこういう本は置けません。
そうですか。
では、私の店にするしかありませんね。
こちらを買い取らせていただきたいのですが。
この店に、こんなに？
これは給料の前払いです。
どちらにしますか？
Both men speak with salesman-to-shopkeeper politeness even as Muranishi buys the store out from under Kitamori. Let's unpack how those polite turns work.
どうぞ。
'Here you go.' "Douzo" is your go-to word whenever you hand something over, motion someone through a door, or invite them to go ahead.
こちらのお店には置いてありませんね。

'You do not carry these in your shop, do you?' "Kochira" literally points 'this way', serving as a polite 'your' in "kochira no omise", your shop. "Oite arimasen" says nothing has been placed in stock.
いや、別に興味はありません。
'No, I am not particularly interested.' Pairing "betsu ni" with a negative ending softens a refusal into 'not really' or 'nothing special', while "kyoumi" means interest.
隠さなくて結構ですよ。
'There is no need to hide it.' Attach "nakute kekkou desu" to a negative stem like "kakusa", from "kakusu", to hide, to say 'you don't need to do that' politely.
うちではこういう本は置けません。
'We cannot stock books like these in our shop.' "Kou iu" means 'this kind of' before "hon", books. Changing "oku", to place, into "okemasen" expresses 'cannot put on the shelves'.
では、私の店にするしかありませんね。
'Then I have no choice but to make this my shop.' "Shika" paired with a negative like "arimasen" means 'nothing except', turning "suru shika arimasen" into 'have no choice but to do'.
こちらを買い取らせていただきたいのですが。

'I would like you to let me buy this place.' "Kaitoru" means to buy out, and stretching it into "kaitorasete itadakitai" humbles the speaker to ask graceful permission—classic Japanese business polish.
これは給料の前払いです。
'This is an advance on your salary.' "Kyuuryou" is a regular job's salary, and "maebarai" joins "mae", front or beforehand, with "harai", payment: paying up front.
どちらにしますか？

'Which one do you choose?' When choosing between two paths, "dochira ni shimasu ka"—literally 'which way will you make it?'—works at a restaurant table and in life-changing deals alike. Now let's listen to the whole bookstore scene again.
どうぞ。
こちらのお店には置いてありませんね。
いや、別に興味はありません。
隠さなくて結構ですよ。
ちょっと待ってください！
うちではこういう本は置けません。
そうですか。
では、私の店にするしかありませんね。
こちらを買い取らせていただきたいのですが。
この店に、こんなに？
これは給料の前払いです。
どちらにしますか？
From ordering lunch to closing a deal, "dochira ni shimasu ka" is a clean, polite way to ask someone which option they choose. See you next time.
また会いましょう。
